game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Drag-and-Drop Simulator. Interactive story at best - not much for a point-and-click adventure.

Owell isn't the first "surveillance sim", and certainly isn't the best. It does plenty of things right, but far more wrong. Because of that, while I enjoyed the game and didn't feel the gameplay bad - I can't recommend it. 

The game holds your hand literally the entire way. It highlights information. It tells you when you've looked over a document and missed something. It repeats the obvious to you via your "advisor", Symes. It doesn't encourage reading whatsoever despite it only having pros as an interactive story.

One of the most irritating things of the game was Symes. Symes is your advisor through the game, commenting on evidence you find. The problem is that he comments on Ever. Little. Piece. of evidence. If you add someone's favorite color - Symes chimes in. If you add a new profile picture for a person - he has something SO IMPORTANT to say that it stops gameplay until you click continue. Again and again and again. 

Other elements of the game leave you wishing you were more in control of the program. For example, I wanted the ability to create profiles on people but you aren't given that permission. Symes gives you permission when you reach a certain point in the story, and that's that. I wanted to add a profile picture for someone I had a profile on..... NOPE couldn't do it until the game gives you permission to.

The game really gives you the illusion of control while the entire time you are limited to dragging and dropping story elements. The conflicts in data are VERY minor and ultimately the story wraps up in a similar way either way. It's the feeling of diverse while being completely linear. In the instances where there WERE conflicts in data, you really have to take a shot in the dark sometimes. 

So what did I expect? I wanted to be in charge of the note taking! I wanted to be able to create profiles on my own. I didn't want information to get highlighted for me UNLESS there was a problem. I wanted to be able to figure things out the entire time without some doofus interrupting gameplay the entire time with his commentary (Symes). 

Still, there are certainly pros to give this game. The story is interesting, the graphics are BEAUTIFUL for the genre, and the point-and-click adventure feel is definitely there, even if the game leads you where you need to go. Browse websites and news articles as though you were in your very own web browser! Now that I say that in writing, it doesn't seem all that impressive, but it's still enjoyable. The "accessing computer" elements and phone conversation elements I enjoy so much more than the web browsing.

All in all, it's an interesting point-and-click interactive story with multiple outcomes. It's not a difficult one, and there are no puzzles to solve, so just sit back and enjoy it. I still can't recommend it to anyone who is a fan of hacksims, surveillance sims, or information gathering sims though.... this is an interactive story - nothing more. It's no more "investigatory" than any of the TellTale games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]English:[/b]
The idea of playing an investigator using a dystopian surveillance system is genuinely intriguing, and it did pull me in at first. But in my case, a few elements caught me off guard, and I ultimately landed on the feeling of, “Damn, this could have been great.”

You're heavily railroaded. A handler constantly directs you, and you're only allowed to submit pre-highlighted data. So even if you spot something meaningful, if it hasn’t been highlighted, it’s off-limits… unless the system decides to highlight it later. In other words, it's Orwell—not your judgment—deciding what's relevant and when.
Also, can’t look into unimportant connections, people connected to the main people you’re already watching. That undermines immersion. Information and connections that should enrich the world instead feel like empty filler, like walking through a map where only the area around your destination actually exists. It undercuts the immersion hard, and it really starts to highlight how little control the player has over the investigation. The joy of organizing fragmented data and piecing together insight, the detective puzzle vibe you’d expect, is barely there.

Even the surveillance state itself feels oddly toothless. Orwell is supposedly a powerful system, yet the most basic info must be found manually. I get that the in-game incident is Orwell's first mission, but if the game is trying to sell a functioning surveillance state, it comes off half-baked.
Starting the investigation from scratch, with no basic personal data preloaded, makes the process resemble ordinary police work more than the operation of a dystopian digital panopticon.

The system’s invasive abilities (like tapping calls or accessing private devices without consent) do hint at Orwell’s dystopian cruelty. But from the player’s point of view, Orwell never allows unrestricted monitoring. Only designated “persons of interest” can be investigated, and since the events revolve around terrorism with real casualties, even the more questionable actions can be framed as emergency measures. This waters down the ethical tension; Orwell’s moral horror feels too easy to rationalize.
Even when one character challenges the legitimacy of Orwell’s power, their argument rings hollow—coming from someone involved in a bombing, it’s hard to see them as anything other than a villain delivering a monologue.

And when the second half of the game shows [spoiler]people casually messing stuff up[/spoiler], it makes you wonder: maybe the surveillance wasn’t that tight to begin with? How effective is this Orwell network if [spoiler]people willing to say "f*ck the system" and can still go full riot mode[/spoiler]? If the system’s that fragile, then what was the point of its supposed success in lowering crime in the first place?
I couldn’t quite tell whether this game was trying to criticize the dystopia built around Orwell or somehow justify it.

Also, you can’t skip or fast-forward dialogue, which I get is supposed to simulate “real-time surveillance,” but it just kills the pacing. This took me about four hours to get through the all chapters, and the lack of any way to redo choices just makes the idea of replaying for achievements or alternate paths a hard no.

[b]日本語:[/b]
ディストピアの監視システムを用いる調査官という導入は凄く面白いし実際に惹き込まれましたが、幾つかの要素が引っ掛かって最終的に「惜しいな」という感想に着地しました。

有り体に言うと意外と(?)自由度が低い。プレイヤーが進行の主導権を握っていないというのが率直な感想です。
まずアドバイザーが就くので情報の海に放り出されて手探りで進むのではなく自然と一本道になるので未知の間を自走する楽しみが希薄です。
更に、二次的な関係者(直接の監視対象ではない人々)の情報には触れられず、例えば誰かの両親や友人等が相関図に載っても飽くまで賑やかしで、RPGで言うなら「目的地周辺だけ作ってあるマップ」みたいな印象を受けるので没入感を削がれます。
そしてOrwellでは“ハイライトされている情報だけ”が利用可能なのですが、例えば関係者の画像を見付けたから登録したいと思ってもハイライトされていないなら使えない――と思いきや後になって急にハイライトされるという事も。つまりシステム(進行度等)の都合で意味の有無が一転してしまうので「役に立つか分からないが留めておきたい」みたいな遊び方は全く想定されておらず、“調査官”という言葉から連想して捜査・整理・推理というパズル的な喜びを期待すると肩透かしを食らいます。

物語や世界観についても引っ掛かります。国民の情報がOrwellに登録されておらず、住所も電話番号も全てプレイヤーが探し出す事になるのは、ゲーム内での事案がOrwellの初陣であるにせよ監視社会のディストピアを念頭に置くなら中途半端な気がしますし、基本的な個人情報から調査となると手順に警察の捜査との差異も感じられません。
Orwellを通じた通話や情報端末への無許可でのアクセスは人権や倫理への一種の加害性というディストピアがディストピアたる所以を描写してはいますが、プレイヤーの視点では上記の通り(=重要人物以外には触れられない) 犯罪や危機の捜査にしか使われておらず、しかも問題となる事件が死傷者を伴うテロなので、倫理観を脇に置くのは超法規的措置だと補完する事も出来てしまう。
その犯人がOrwellを非難したところで犠牲者を生んだテロリストの言説として空虚に響くだけでしょう。
また[spoiler]後半での展開も炎上からの破壊行動が容易く起きるのなら[/spoiler]“監視”の程度も大した事はないのでは？と感じます。監視なんぞ知るかという人が[spoiler]暴徒化したのだとしたら[/spoiler]、そもそも犯罪率の低下とは何だったんでしょうか。
正直なところ、この作品がOrwellに在る社会構造を否定的に描いているのか肯定的に描いているのか判然としませんでした。

実績や細かい分岐の確認に改めてプレイしていたら印象も変わるのかもしれませんが、ここでシステム面が障害に。というのも、だいぶのんびりしたプレイで全5章終わらせるのに約4時間掛かったのですが、Orwellには台詞送りやスキップ機能がなく、更には選択に修正が効かない仕様なのでリプレイへの精神的なハードルが高いです。
台詞送りやスキップが無いのはリアルタイムの盗聴という表現であるにしても快適性を損ないますし、こういった部分も作品の魅力を自ら削いでいる様な感じがしてなりません。

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Disappointing.  

1. Incredibly short.  I was surprised when it was over, as it felt like I just completed a tutorial.
2. Hand holding the entire way through.  Your "adviser" or "controller" does just that, controls you.  All you do is drag and drop things.  You make very few decisions and are spoon fed what you need to do next.
3. Worse than number 2, you are spoon fed what to think and make of your findings.  Rather than allowing you to actually investigate and figure things out, the game tells you precisely what to think.  This kills immersion and makes you, not an investigator, but just a peon dragging and dropping lines of text.
4. Game locked up for me on conclusion.  I have only played through one ending and have no desire to do the others, because the gameplay is like a tutorial from start to finish.  It would be tedious as hell playing through it again.
5. Writing is corny.  It feels like it is forcing the dialogue to be edgy and using memes.  Seriously feels like an awful episode of BBT.

So much potential, but fails the entire way through.  Definitely not worth 10 pounds.  Not even worth 5.  Maybe 1.99.  The game is incredibly short.  Steam says I played it for 7.1 hours, but the reality is I fell asleep while playing about halfway through and dozed off for a couple hours.  Even at 7 hours, the gameplay is disappointingly short.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While the story is interesting and I can see replayability in knowing you've made the wrong move, then creating a new profile and trying to avoid that scenario... I haven't done that. I probably won't either, because I have to agree with other players: the game guides you too much.

You're basically told where to click and when, which completely defeats the point of having all of these fun tools at your disposal--they might as well have dumped all data pieces in a list and had you click on them one by one, all after the other.

The auto-highlighting spoils the point of reading anything. The game warns you that potential choices conflict instead of letting the player decide on how thoroughly they want to investigate before submitting information. Some pieces of info feel completely useless, but your supervisor somehow decides they have more value than they should and the supervisor's decision often feels like a complete whim. And vice-versa: bits of info you feel should be important are locked away or not even meant to be accessible because the game decided "Nope, I won't even let you go into that dead-end for fun".

I guess this was worth what I paid for it... $2! and no more. This had a lot of promise but it doesn't have enough depth or freedom of choice for my tastes.

This is not a good game. Firstly it tells you what to do and you cant progress if you don't follow those orders. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell's design does a good job at disguising the fact that it is pretty much basically just a very fancy visual novel. This isn't really a huge deal because it's still pretty entertaining, but there's not a whole lot of game in this game. Your advisor tells you pretty much everything you need to do and then like a cog in a machine, you just do it. 
There's a sorta hamfisted political message that it presents well and fairly subtly initally, but then fumbles towards the end of the game. It goes well with the story.
The one issue that I found to be pretty damaging with Orwell is that for such a story driven game, I didn't feel any emotions towards the characters. They're pretty average archetypes that are awkwardly written, as if one talented writer wrote the framework for the game and another less talented writer wrote the dialogue. The only real connection I formed was with the advisor character, which was just a shell for nearly 90% of the game, as a way to inject tutorial into the story without breaking immersion. 

I hope you like reading, because it's about 6 hours worh of reading.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1][i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye One You’s[/i] centrism recklessly justifies surveillance[/h1]

[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] (Osmotic Studios, 2016) should not have to prove that mass surveillance is a public danger. Lifting the name of one of the 20th century’s most enduring authors, [i]Orwell[/i] reverses the traditional dystopian power dynamic by casting the player as an investigator utilizing government software to snoop on anyone deemed potentially dangerous to the state. The setup is almost too clean to be proper satire, too on the nose to spark the outrage necessary to criticize what is fast becoming a common aspect of life.

Across the globe, [url=https://www.amnesty.org.uk/north-korea-surveillance-state-prison-camp-internet-phone-technology]authoritarian[/url] and [url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/graphics/2020/world/national-security/cia-crypto-encryption-machines-espionage/]democratic governments[/url] alike have begun [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/9kx4z8/revealed-this-is-palantirs-top-secret-user-manual-for-cops?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]adopting surveillance technology[/url] under the [url=https://www.vice.com/en_us/article/k7exem/banjo-ai-company-utah-surveillance-panopticon?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]premise of reducing crime[/url]. Few of these programs have detailed exactly what data is being collected and how it is being used, but journalists have exposed many of the ways surveillance programs are only [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/05/technology/clearview-investors.html?utm_source=pocket&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=pockethits]further stratifying power along class[/url] and [url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/612876/this-is-how-ai-bias-really-happensand-why-its-so-hard-to-fix/]racial lines[/url]. The dystopia is already here. The role of fiction is no longer to provide warnings and speculation, it’s to interrogate our current reality.

[i]Orwell[/i] released less than five years ago, but it is shocking how tame its surveillance state looks compared to how corporations and governments are currently operating (and in all likelihood, how they were spying in years prior). For starters, its system is structured to rely on human intuition rather than artificial intelligence. Data points are only considered after they’ve been entered by the investigator, after which supervisors are required to act upon them even to the point of self-incrimination.

Orwell, the program, is portrayed as an equalizing arbiter of justice. Only late in the game is the idea floated that the investigators are being watched too. But by that time the system has already been a resounding success. Lives have been saved and poorly coordinating terrorists are behind bars. If [i]Orwell[/i] intended to question the merit of a nationwide police state, it accidentally proved the other side’s point. In this reality, the only reason to oppose surveillance is that it feels icky to have your phones tapped and your computers bugged.

But this isn’t how surveillance functions, or how these systems are run. Almost universally, modern surveillance technology is autonomous, relying on millions of data points to infer what the system believes a crime to be. This has enormous ramifications when the criminal justice [url=http://inthesetimes.com/working/entry/17505/police_and_poor_people]system disproportionally targets people of color and the poor[/url]. Facial recognition has already been proven to possess the same biases as the system utilizing it, which is to say nothing of the exceptions granted to the wealthy and other members of power.

In [i]Orwell*, the terrorists are strictly ideological. They are educated, wealthy, white, heterosexual philosophers waging a war of ideas that almost by accident turns violent. These people exist, sure, but they are not the ones targeted by surveillance systems. That *Orwell[/i] utterly ignores any possibility of racial and ethnic biases or the role history plays in policing, renders the whole game hollow and borderline optimistic. None of the characters the player investigates are innocent. Orwell is infallible, even if its implementation is unnerving.

The final bizarre and revealing element [i]Orwell[/i] is how little it allows the player to deviate from what the system believes to be relevant. Play involves parsing documents and dragging relevant information over to profiles, but the only pieces of data which can be included are ones the game has highlighted in advance.

This begs the question as to why the player is there. Is it to catch the extremely rare instance of irrelevant data being entered into the system (ie. a person’s favorite color)? If so, why does the supervisor ultimately decide what is and isn’t relevant? Are they meant to be an impartial judge of the people being investigated? Why, then, does the system decide what information can be considered in a case?

[i]Orwell[/i] tries to introduce safeguards into the surveillance operation but in doing so further highlights how futile these measures are in protecting from false imprisonment and machine bias. If we are beginning the conversation at “how do we ethically implement a mass surveillance system” we have already lost. It is not a question of how it can be done, it is a question of how we could allow it to happen. These systems exist. They are being used. Hell, even [url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/19/opinion/facebook-cambridge-analytica.html]Facebook operates in ways indistinguishable from police surveillance[/url] and might be more successful for it.

Games like [i]Orwell[/i] recklessly attempt to work backward from the lies used to justify surveillance, rather than recognizing that we have to fight the concept itself. It is a game decades too late to matter and does more to legitimize its target than it does to take them down.

///

review_text_raw:
At first I was intrigeud by the concept of the game but after 30 minutes of gameplay it felt more like a guided tour than an interactive experience. 

The game starts with CCTV footage of a bombing at a plaza. In that footage a woman who has a criminal record is identified. From her you will start your investigation. The game presents you with newspaper articles, web pages as well as personal communication logs in which you will find marked passages of text or pictures, so called data junks, which you can upload to an agency to complete a person profile as well as finding connections to other people. 

Unfortunately you can't upload information which the game itself deems unrelevent. Some information which is rather useless needs to be uploaded to progress. Some information will even be taken out of context and there is nothing you can do than upload it and watch your handler making the wrong asumptions.

In one instance you have the profile of a person without the picture. You will find that persons picture very soon but will be unable to upload it. In another instance a data junk you can upload will be totally out of context from the conversation it can be taken. The worst was that on time where I could not upload proof of a direct connection beween a persons statement and the letter of intent which was sent to a ploice department prior to the bombing. Ironicly, at the very beginning, the game warns you to make sure not to upload anything that might be misleading or irellevant.

If you are looking for a story in wich you just press highlighted pieces of text to progress this might be the game for you. If you where hoping for a game in wich you are asked to find out what happened using online surveilance you might want to look somewhere else.

review_text_raw:
Pitched as a mystery/investigation game, but really it's a glorified Visual Novel - rather than actually doing any of the investigating/hacking promised in the description, you're spoon-fed a linear progression of information. You have some agency on which to hand in, but only pre-selected bits, and most are necessary to progress. 

Buy it if you're looking for a mostly linear narrative, not if you're actually looking to play a detective game.

[h1]I wouldn't even pirate it/10[/h1]

90% of the game is clicking and dragging stuff, fair enough, might even sound playable until here.
50% of the clicking is skipping the dialogue of your annoying "advisor" which just has to fucking have an opinion about every single little thing you drag around. So now the hacker and the terrorist motivator beg you and the game lets you choose between framing the terrorists and exposing the government for keeping track of the terrorists.

Actual playtime was 2.5 hours. I afk'd a bit more for steam trading cards. Stay away from this. Not even worth the 3 euros.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Okay... I don't usually write game reviews. I generally have a pretty good idea of what I'm buying beforehand on Steam, and if a game is shit it's usually because I paid for shit. But this fucking game got me.

The biggest trick is that little "Choice Matters" tag that people gave it. I love choice games. The replay value of finding every unique ending alone usually makes it worth the price. There's also something thrilling, something special to video games, when you're able to make a choice and know it matters.

Choice doesn't matter in this game.

You do ultimately get to choose what's "shown" to your supervisor, and sometimes those choices do affect the game in some way. But you're railroaded HARD through just about every major event, forced to fight for even the smallest change in dialogue from game to game. The only half-consequential "choice" you get comes at the end, and to get there you need to sit through 2+ hours of the exact same gameplay. You might as well be buying the game to play once. If you're ok with playing once and then quitting (the game does have some beautiful artwork and some really gripping moments) then by all means do so. But if you want your choices to really matter, don't buy Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I played this game through once, and am surprised to read so many positive reviews, especially about the witing and characterisation which was weak, cliched and overall, spoilt my sense of immersion. 


I felt railroaded by this game- especially by your "advisor" who is constantly interrupting with inane nonsense. I rarely felt as though my choices seemed to matter. More so at the end, but by then I'd already resigned myself to the fact that this was an experience, not a game. 


The story itself was fine, and I like the general idea and premise of the game- putting you in the role of the investigator, making decisions which would cause the lives or deaths of the people you were investigating in, what must be seen as, a morally dubious way. 

The problem is, I never really did feel as though I was investigating, because for at least the first two days the game completely spoon feeds you, and feels as though nothing you do matters- the course of the story is inevitable. I don't mind being railroaded, but the game should at least have the illusion of choice. Every "data chunk" you upload causes something else to beep, leading you to the next. There is very little true decision making till the last day. 

Another problem is the extremely weak cast of characters who are all based on familiar and unimaginative stereotypes: the rebellious rich girl, the arrogant rockboy agintant, the foriegn professor with a mysterious past. The stereotypes might have been passable if it were not for the atociously written dialogue, which felt more like a high school drama conducted entiely by people with sub-par IQs. I found myself disliking all the characters and being irritated by the dialogue which so clearly served an agenda to ilucidate parts of the plot, instead of giving any sense of them being real people with real motivations. 

I also found the constant interruptions, the slow type speed of the conversations to be obnoxiously aggravating. The "assistant" rarely says anything of actual worth, and when taking data chunks in mid-conversation I really wish I could have switched him off, or the developers had limited his appearence. I also found the way that all new or unread data pinged up and highlighted in red meant that I almost never needed to think. I am sure that you could complete this game in a foriegn language just by clicking where the game told you, without understanding a single word of what's written. 

Now, having said all of this, I bought the game on sale and it's cheap. 5 hours of play time for £3.50- I guess there is a limit to what you can expect a studio to produce for that sort of budget. I'm pleased I didn't pay £7 for it though. 


Overall I think it's a poor handling of a great concept, and thus a wasted opportunity.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Orwell fails on a lot of levels. A lot of very fundamental writing levels. First and foremost it gives you a set of tools that allow you to see what people do on the internet and tasks you with finding the perpetrator of a bombing. You're given one prime suspect and as you progress your web of people of interest grows and grows. The principle gameplay mechanic involves choosing which specific pieces of information you choose to report to your orwellian system. Which will change how the game plays out. The first failure comes that it is often very obvious what information is going to affect what, as it is all highlighted in blue, or yellow if it conflicts with another piece of information. This is another problem. The conflict system makes very little sense most of the time. One of the first examples of the system in use involves a personal blog ran by a Person of Interest and an editorial they wrote for a newspaper. They both detail the same concept but with completely differeing opinions on the matter, and these pieces of information are considered a conflict and therefore cannot both be reported. While this specific instance makes very little gameplay difference either way it still makes no sense. Being able to report both pieces of information would have shown (at least to me) his willingness to play whatever side of an issue would get him paid, and could've sowed him as a much stronger suspect later on. Instead you have instances where you handler is confused by information you weren't able to provide them due to it being a conflict, when both pieces of information were true. This creates a very frustrating experience in trying to influence the story and with trying to keep information that is relevant to the story seperate from information that isnt. Another fundamental failing of the story telling is its ending, which if I'm perfectly honest; is godawful. To my knowledge, your choices throughout the game have no impact on the ending. There's just three buttons at the end. Push one for your ending. None of them making  a bit of sense. Right before your ending the perpetrator of the bombings reveals themselves, showing that the previous three chapters had all just been misdirection to make sure no player could possibly guess the real one and they basically say to you the player "And this is why your system doesn't work! You couldn't even figure out I was the perpetrator" When it was the game mechanics and information that was provided to you by the game that made it impossible to determine the perpetrator. They then ask you to take down the system, since you can now see it doesnt work. your other two options are to get a politician associated with your orwell system arrested, or to claim the group the perpetrator belongs to are all terrorists using out of context IMs. If you're thinking that this seems to be lacking a very obvious fourth option then I agree. My first instinct was simply to use the perpetrator admitting to instigating the bombings to get her arrested. As that would make sense, she admitted it to our face and yet there's no option present. Just the three arbitrary ones presented. In the end it was three chapters of intriguing build up for one chapter of letdowns and unguessable twists that completely kill the narrative, suspension of disbelief, and immersion. 4/10

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is a dishonest indictment against current surveilance and privacy ethics. It tries to force you into an unethical position so that it can pull off a "gotcha" moment for emotional impact and cheap pedantic morals. You play the nameless analyst that feeds the State with information about people trying to prevent crimes through surveilance of private communications and crossreference of public sources. So far so good. The problems start when the writers remove player agency and predestine outcomes. This happens in two ways.

1) The game uses a system of "conflicting data chunks" which are SUPPOSEDLY contradictory information pieces and you have to judge which is the correct one. Only they aren't. Say that you ram a car in a crossroad in rage. And you do it because you know that this car is going to kill your parents in the next stop. Are these contradictory? Well for this game they are. And you get different outcomes if you select one or the other to "push" to your supervisor. This is called lazy writing and removes player agency. Moving on...

2) You work a narrative case to your best judgement and then the game robs you of an outcome that is as obvious as a billboard on a busy highway. Say that you have a classic crime procedural where the detective is trying to break a suspect. Imagine the detective knows that the suspect is ethical and peaceful and that there is going to be a murder unless the suspect gives up a criminal acquaintance. The expected narrative would be to appeal to humanity and have a reasonable resolution. But no. The game, having known that you did not went for the "cog in the machine" trope, for cheap emo guilt trips, pulls a gotcha and just blows the murder on your face saying you "failed".

At the time of writing this review there is an article in Kotaku about "ludo-narrative dissonance", i.e. how gameplay conflicts with narrative. (link: https://kotaku.com/the-bioshock-problem-when-gameplay-and-narrative-clash-1847698124). This, sometimes can be a good thing as it might shed light into serious ethical conundrums for the player. 
Here the attempt fails because the writers and designers went pedantic and decided to rob the players of even the off chance to experience a story where things would plausibly move in a more nuanced direction than the beat to death pseudo-dilemma "bad state vs bad people" and "security vs freedom". 

Instead of exploring the grey area of these ethics they threw every stereotype in the book to the player and plain and simple punished them when they did not conform to their teenage black and white mentality. 

It's a pity, the review is coming late, but don't bother...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
For a game of mostly dialogue, the writing is pretty bad. Dialogues are full of cliches, characters are incredibly unlikeable, especially the first character you investigate who is just a narcissistic turd. If anything, the game makes a compelling argument FOR a nanny state, because these people all suck. I also have no clue why you have a handler, as all they do is say the most inane, mindless, stupid things whenever you upload a clue. Upload a person's interest in hiking and "Oh, she likes to go outside. Interesting." It's like the most boring person in the world is looking over your shoulder watching you work and commenting. 

The gameplay is also pretty deceptive. It makes it seem like you can omit information and be subversive, but some information is required to move forward, and you don't know which until the game just stops moving forward. So if you wanted to make someone seem like they aren't a terrorist or are, you can't. Which felt like the whole point of the game? A lot of decisions, like choosing which person's photo is on their dossier, are entirely irrelevant. It's just padding to make it seem like you are doing more than you are. In fact, most of the choices you make aren't choices. The ending also gets to the exact same climax regardless.

Also a weird decision to highlight the relevant sections to upload. I was essentially just skimming every document for the highlighted bit and going 'okay, that's the part that matters' and ignoring the rest. I say this as a person that likes to read, but because it hand holds you, you just click on the tab it tells you to click (with a helpful red exclamation mark) then click the text it tells you to click, and if there ever IS a decision, like two conflicting pieces of information that might make someone seem bad, it helpfully tells you not to make a mistake and wait until you get more info to submit that info, basically cutting out the only agency you might have as a player.

Good idea, but executed poorly.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In Orwell you sit in front of a virtual computer screen and attempt to track down the perpetrators of a recent bombing in an authoritarian surveillance state (hence the name of the game).

Set in the fictitious country of The Nation, you play The Investigator, someone employed from outside The Nation to work on its secret interior security project called Orwell. You receive verbal communiques one-way from your supervisor, who directs you on what to do. In return you send back snippets of information you find online.

In the aftermath of a bombing in Freedom Plaza (ironic name, geddit?), you must track down the perpetrators. You start from a single person arrested at the scene, and trace out her social and familial connections to bring more and more people under scrutiny. 

The Orwell computer system allows you to potentially pry into all aspects of a character's online life, as long as you can find a link to enable you to uncover each new aspect. You can look through public websites, but also snoop on messaging conversations, phone calls and email, as well as later being able to access the characters' computers themselves and have a nose around.

Certain information you come across is highlighted, what the game calls "data chunks", and you either provide these to your supervisor, or withhold them, to build a profile on someone and direct the security services to a conclusion about their guilt or innocence in the bombing.

It's a reasonable idea. However, to progress in the game, you have to throw out any common-sense notions you might have about how the information you provide will be interpreted, because it frequently defies any sense. 

The game makes it clear in the beginning that many of the "data chunks" are understood by your supervisor in their full context, but then all of a sudden something you pass along about a character referring jokingly to the "torture" of being dragged on a night out by a friend is taken completely out of context as referring to literal torture. The game tells you that information "uploads" into Orwell cannot be undone, but they also cannot be clarified.

Some "data chunks" are highlighted in a different colour, which you learn means that it conflicts with at least one other piece of information out there in cyberspace. You are only allowed to upload one of these pieces of information into the system, because it is a necessary game mechanic that the investigators cannot handle two or more possibilities for a biographic detail, so you have to pick one to send along. 

Someone might say that is how it is supposed to be, but these things feel forced as you play the game. It is especially frustrating because you often do not get any indication as to how each piece of information you decide should be taken for granted will affect what happens next.

Game events are seemingly triggered by your uploading information. This puts you in the position of uploading information you thought extraneous, or otherwise wished to withhold, in an effort to get the game to advance by finding the right trigger.

In the final act, you see written in what characters have said choices for an outcome. However, it is not clear how you are supposed to enact what I imagine for most players would be the desired outcome, nor does the character's explanation of how that outcome shall come about make sense.

Despite all of the references to Orwell's 1984, the comparison between The Nation and Oceania would be a lazy one. This is a game to suit someone who has only heard of 1984, and not actually read it. Where the extent of their understanding of the work is that that Big Brother fellow liked his surveillance. 

In the game, The Nation is authoritarian, but non-ideological. There is something about it being pro-interventionist and anti-immigration, but this does not serve as an effective allegory about real-world politics. Although the beastly Orwell programme reaches far into people's private lives, its administrators are awfully concerned with ethics and the rule of law. They have to gain legal warrants to bring someone under the scrutiny of the system, and are annoyed by your giving them extraneous personal detail. 

Although some important legal protections for the accused are absent, accused people are apparently entitled to legal representation. There is no indication that the state much cares about what people think, or that it coerces them into changing. That is, there are no thought crimes in The Nation, and state power is not arbitrary or lawless. Rather, its inhabitants appear to have have freedom of speech, thought and assembly (and, it seems from one plot point, the right to bear arms).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Thoughts[/h1]

So let start off with saying I purchased the full game after playing the demo, looking back the demo actually offers everything that you would find in the main game so I would highly suggest playing the demo before making a purchase and understand that the gameplay isnt any different.

The premise of the game is to locate pertinent information about certain suspects in response to a terror attack, the information is uploaded to a system for your superior to review. The superior talks to pretty much every time you upload something, questioning the information and how it can be used against them.  The communication is totally one way and unfortunately because of the limited information you can upload sometimes it is taken very much out of context. e.g. someone was torturing someone else with muffins…. Uploading this to the system and the superior freaked out saying this person needs investigating because they like to torture people.  Hmm, I get that is the game design but yeah it’s a bit bizarre.

I use the term locate here very loosely because the game essentially spoon feeds you documents, links and webpages that contains the important information, the task at hand is to determine if the information is actually useful or not.  Every now and then you get some information which conflicts and you have to upload just one piece of information however this type of interaction doesn’t happen that often which is a shame.

I also didn’t like how the story abruptly ended, it wasn’t obvious in any way that if I upload this bit of information the game would finish.  I was taken completely by surprise and I understand there are multiple endings available but the choice just wasn’t obvious.

Despite playing the demo I still assumed the game would offer a lot more detective work later on, I assumed that I would need to locate web pages, search people and scan the documents but no.  The system finds everything and then sends you it gift tied in a little star shaped parcel.  All you do is drag and drop blue text to the box on the left and occasionally choose between one bit of yellow text and another bit of yellow text.

Overall I think this game offers great potential but it falls down with its boring repetitive gameplay that require zero thought or analysis.  If you are wanting a detective text based game look at Hacknet, for me that that is far superior to this as its on you to find and locate the information rather than it being spoon fed to you.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
An ultimately disappointing game. It's very short (~3 hours for a full run even if you are taking your time and reading everything), which I can forgive if the game is excellent but it's not.

The gameplay itself, as others have noted, is drag-and-drop pre-highlighted bits of text. Some of this text is mandatory for the game to proceed, some of it is optional. It's not always clear which, so it's easy to get stuck if you are doing a replay and want to see what happens if you ignore bits of evidence, and you may accidentially find yourself doing the same thing that you did last time.

A lot of the choices you make (up until episode 5) are relatively inconsequential, you'll get different text but the overall plot remains the same. Unfortunately there's no way to replay an episode to see what would happen if you did something else; supposedly this feature is being worked on, but in a choice-driven game this should have been a feature that shipped; Tell Tale has had this feature since The Walking Dead season 1.

I thought this game was going to be more about the surveillance state ala 1984, Person of Interest, etc. but I wouldn't say this is a good critique. True, you are reading other people's emails, but we're not investigating some political dissidents who said bad things about Great Leader, we're investigating an actual in-universe violent incident (and someone who potentially wants to commit more of these.) So while snooping through the emails of the suspects, it's not unreasonable to think that you are trying to catch people who legitimately committed a real crime. The game does try to railroad you a bit to force you to investigate someone who may not be the offender, which you can ignore, but this is pretty late in the game.

Some of the story beats just don't work; for instance, in the final parts of episode 4, [spoiler]information about your handler is leaked and the game forces you to drag-drop some of his personal information into his file. There's zero reason to actually do this, it's only to force the user to involve someone who clearly isn't a related to the crimes. And that would work if it was optional, but it's not. It's a "you are meant to feel bad right now" bit, and just falls flat.[/spoiler]

The "good ending" is pretty trash, [spoiler]everyone sings the freedom song and topples down statues and gives you a plaque for spilling the beans, ask Snowden how that's working out for him. It's rather corny.[/spoiler]

Overall had decent potential and the demo (episode 1) is pretty good, but fails in the end stretch.

Instead being serious he acted like someone who just finished College or studied Criminology and ended up with comments like - We will get them bruh! I don't believe in coincidence, bruh! FFS, Symes I am “reading” (there is no actual Voiceover, recorded sound of conversation, they are automatically show as text) phone call.[/spoiler] What I want to say, when this advisor shows in - screen turns grey and background is unresponsive (you cannot scroll pages) until you click on his text bubble.

“20 datachunk -make it count”  game fragment
Multiple choices for suspect [spoiler]Nina Maternova[/spoiler] and [spoiler]show of stupidity of incorrectly interpreting received data[/spoiler]
At the ending part, you see there is over 100 pages with written content

For that price SHORT

Poor writing (specially I wish I could mute adviser)

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Running on PopOS Linux (and this game has a linux client)... crashed on activating the first achievement.

Which is about the time I was ready to walk away from the game anyway.

Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

review_text_raw:
I bought it after the RPS recommended it and... yeah it was one big disappointment... I didn't even finish it as it was so boring. The story is boring, the gameplay is boring, the graphics are eye hurting. Seriously if you are able to read quickly you will bore to death in this game. I was waiting for the texts to comin or for the calls to finish. As far as I can see the game is linear and there's an apparence of choice that is just an illusion. After the predictable ending of chapter 3 I said no more and uninstalled the game. 

Don't buy it. not even for the 3-4 hours of gameplay. I understand what the devs wanted to show - the ever present invigilation of govt in our lives and that taking things out of context can end very badly.Perhaps the problem is that I went in thinking this game would be like papers please - it's not. 

There is no game here at all, none. Instead, it's about dragging blue text onto peoples records, and then your supervisor, who speaks less with the tone of a long time bureaucrat that is spying on people, and more like a wet blanket that instantly talks with you extremely casually. Worst still, it makes government surveillance severely underpowered compared to reality.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I love the game mechanics!

However, I wish the game gave players more power to decide what actions to take.

Since you’re just an information collector, the only way to influence the outcome is by choosing not to feed certain information to your supervisor. That limits a lot of freedom because you can't really control what a scripted supervisor thinks. And sometimes, if you don’t feed the plot-required information, the game just stops and waits for you, forcing you to still somewhat follow the intended plot. The illusion of "choice matter" in this case is worse than reading a visual novel.

This game is a play style I would enjoy. Unfortunately I'm stuck on the very first/tutorial level. I've gotten all the data points I can from every source. My Supervisor said he was going to alert authorities ... and that's all the game did. I've clicked back through every page of every, thing, I can. I've re-read every article and text message, but there's nothing left to do. 

Check the discussions. Lots of players hit points in the game where progression stops. You either have to click around all the screens until something happens, uninstall and reinstall the game, or just give up. I've clicked everywhere, I'm not in the mood to reinstall this one; so I give up

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Tries way too hard to be punchy or meaningful, to the point where its intended messages kind of feel spoonfed to the player. Characters in the story and the dialogue between them also feels silly and surreal in an unpleasant way. Having Symes pop up to give his input at every line of info you drop into Orwell feels abrupt and disrupts the flow of the game. This distracts from the gameplay pretty heavily. I enjoy the gameplay itself though. The conflicting information you're given, challenges you to scrutinise small details about the context of the "data-chunks" in order to record the most accurate information. It doesn't do this enough throughout the game though. I've played through to the end of Chapter 4, but I've lost interest and can't be bothered playing through to the end of the game. 

Tl;dr: Orwell makes you feel smart, and dumb, but mostly dumb.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: I received this game for free as part of the HumbleBumble sale so i am not too bothered about value for money but, if i had paid for it, I would be very disapointed. The actual story is very short; it took me about 3 hours to complete and a large majority of this time is take up by unskipable "Phone calls" you have to sit through and read, yes... read; there are no voice actors so this is basically a text game with some fancy graphics. For example at the end you are forced into reading a 8min long phone call and you can't do anything else. The actual story itself seems very unintresting. [spoiler] There are 3 bombings and you have to figure out who did it. Seems intresting? WRONG! You are spoonfed this woman who hapens to be a part of this group. Then you drag and drop some info, find out some members and then it turns out they did it. There is no thought needed for the story.[/spoiler]
